structure.title: Structure (ISO 3779)
structure.explain: The first three characters identify the manufacturer, characters 4–9 describe the vehicle, and 10–17 identify the individual unit. Only the manufacturer-specific middle part varies between makers — that is why a decoder needs several data sources.
structure.smallManufacturer: Small-series manufacturer (fewer than 1000 vehicles per year)

vin.title: What is a Vehicle Identification Number (VIN)?
vin.body1: A VIN is the unique code a manufacturer assigns to a vehicle during production. It has exactly 17 characters. The letters I, O and Q never appear — they are too easy to confuse with the digits 1 and 0.
vin.body2: The code is standardised by ISO 3779 and ISO 3780, but only its structure is. What the individual characters mean in the middle section is defined by each manufacturer separately, which is why decoding needs more than one data source.
vin.where: On the driver's side of the dashboard, visible through the windscreen; on the vehicle registration document; and stamped into the chassis — the type approval record even states the exact position for each model.

anatomy.title: How a VIN is put together
anatomy.vdsText: Model, body and engine — manufacturer-specific, not standardised.
anatomy.checkText: Mandatory in North America and China; in Europe usually a filler character.
anatomy.yearText: Repeats every 30 years, so it is never unambiguous on its own.
anatomy.plantText: The assembly plant, defined by the manufacturer.
anatomy.serialText: Identifies the individual vehicle. This tool never stores it.

legacy.title: Before 1981 the VIN was not standardised
legacy.body: Every manufacturer used its own format, so length and structure varied widely. The 17-character format has been mandatory since 1981. For older vehicles the manufacturer has to be known — the structural rules below do not apply to them.

yearTable.title: Model year codes (position 10)
yearTable.body: The tenth character encodes the model year in a 30-year cycle. This table comes from the same source the decoder itself uses, so it cannot drift apart from the actual result.

countryTable.title: Country ranges of the manufacturer identifier
countryTable.body: The first two characters determine the country of production under ISO 3780. Shown here are the ranges our decoder actually evaluates.

facts.letters: I, O and Q, to avoid confusion with 1 and 0
facts.sourceTitle: Where do the technical data come from?
facts.source: Swiss type approvals (ASTRA TARGA), published as open government data

eu.title: What is an EU type approval?
eu.body: Type approval is the procedure that confirms a vehicle type meets European safety, environmental and technical requirements before it may be sold. The authority tests one sample; the manufacturer then confirms that every unit built matches that approved type, so individual vehicles do not have to be tested.
eu.findTitle: Where to find the approval number
eu.find1: On the manufacturer's plate — usually in the engine bay, on a door pillar or under the bonnet.
eu.find2: On the vehicle registration document, in most EU countries.
eu.find3: On the Certificate of Conformity (CoC) issued by the manufacturer.
eu.part1: Country that granted the approval (e1 = Germany, e2 = France)
eu.part2: Base directive or regulation (2007/46 = framework directive)
eu.part3: Sequential number of the base approval
eu.why1: A vehicle with EU type approval can be registered in any member state without further technical inspection.
eu.why2: It guarantees that safety and emission standards were met before the vehicle reached the road.
eu.why3: The approval record is what makes it possible to look up engine, transmission and emission data from a chassis number at all.
